newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire and rebels drift further apart on peace plan.
newsitem.headline: Zaire and rebels drift further apart on peace plan.

text.p: Rebels thrusting deeper in eastern Zaire on Thursday rejected the government's call for international monitors to help implement a U.N. truce plan.
The government in turn again ruled out negotiations between ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko and rebel leader Laurent Kabila, who links a ceasefire to such talks.

"Kabila is a mere puppet. How can President Mobutu negotiate with him while it's known that he is only a front man for the aggressors," Deputy Foreign Minister Lokondo Yoka told reporters in the capital Kinshasa.

"Zaire has been attacked by Rwanda, Burundi and Uganda," he said. "If any Zairean who opposes the regime can take up arms to seize power with the support of foreign countries, this would be unfortunate."
On Thursday French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette accused Uganda directly of intervening in Zaire.
But he indicated France, which wants U.N. intervention to stop hostilities in a move that could save Mobutu's crumbling authority, would not act alone in Zaire.

"We demand the respect of Zaire's territorial integrity. What must stop are the interventions of its neighbours, particularly Uganda whose activity on Zairean soil is an established fact," de Charette told the newspaper Ouest-France.
Zaire's three neighbours deny that their troops are fighting alongside Tutsi-led rebels who took up arms in October and have seized a large stretch of eastern Zaire borderland.

As rebel forces appeared closing in on the government army's operational base in the city of Kisangani, Zaire on Wednesday called for the monitors and abruptly agreed a U.N. ceasefire plan that it had dismissed last month as timid.

"International monitors could become an interposition force and it would just result once again in the protection of Mobutu Sese Seko by his foreign friends," rebel justice minister Mwenze Kongolo told Reuters.
Mobutu, 66, seized power in Zaire in 1965 but is now in Europe where he had surgery for prostate cancer last August.
Kenya said on Thursday it would host a summit on the Zaire conflict on March 19 but made it clear Kabila and sympathetic governments in Uganda and Rwanda would not be invited.
The rebels shrugged off the apparent snub, saying they did not expect anything of value from Moi's summit anyway.

"We have always said clearly that nothing could come out of a summit in Nairobi, Moi is part of the conflict because he has always been such a close ally of Mobutu Sese Seko," Mwenze said in Kindu, the latest major town to fall to the rebels.
Kenyan foreign ministry spokesman David Kikaya said Kenya had asked Mobutu to attend the one-day talks with South Africa's Nelson Mandela and five other African heads of state.
"The purpose of the summit is to advance the search for peace and a lasting solution in eastern Zaire," Kikaya told Reuters in Nairobi.

Rebel centres were meanwhile being flooded by youths wanting to enlist in the guerrilla force. Would-be recruits turning up at rebel posts in Kindu, which fell to the rebels on Sunday, were told to leave their names and return when a recruitment programme was organised locally.

In Nairobi, a WFP spokeswoman said planes ferrying food to the town of Punia confirmed Rwandan Hutu refugees were arriving in Ubundu, 130 km (80 miles) northwest of Tingi Tingi and 100 km (60 miles) south of the northeastern capital of Kisangani.
Some 170,000 refugees fled from Tingi Tingi last Friday.
